A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same HLP study despite retitling and reformatting. All pages, including appendices, equations, figures and tables, are readable and support reliable matching.

before.justification: v2 reports original controlled training experiments, benchmark evaluations, horizon-awareness probing and appendix ablations.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds attention analysis, planning-error measurements, nonlinear probing, loss-weight sensitivity and self-infilling evaluations.

M1.justification: The normalized horizon target, linear sigmoid head, L1 auxiliary loss and combined training objective remain unchanged. The separate L2R horizon-prediction adaptation already appears in v2 Appendix A.1 and is retained in v3 A.5. Self-infilling is an additional evaluation procedure.

E1.justification: The four training languages and existing evaluation datasets and tasks are retained. HumanEval already appears in v2's appendix; the new self-infilling experiment changes decoding within that existing task. The less specific training-subset description does not establish different data coverage.

E2.justification: The NTP controls and original ablation comparators remain. The four-token multi-token-prediction comparison moves from v2 Section 5.1/Table 6 to v3 Appendix A.3/Table 10 unchanged. Self-infilling supplies a shared decoding procedure for the NTP-versus-HLP comparison.

E3.justification: v3 substantially extends evaluation procedures: a 100K-step loss-weight sweep, nonlinear probing, suffix-attention ratios, an operational ordering-error test, and greedy self-infilling with zero to four refinement loops. These are additional designs; the retained benchmark experiments keep their original protocols and 200K-step training budget.

E4.justification: Beyond v2's linear probe, multi-token comparison and design ablations, v3 adds analyses of suffix attention and misplaced final lines, tests nonlinear recoverability of horizon information, examines loss-weight sensitivity, and studies self-infilling refinement. These substantially broaden the evidence investigating HLP's mechanism and robustness.

E5.justification: Both versions retain paired t-tests with p < 0.05, the same significance markers, and sampling counts of 10 for CRUXEval and 200 for EvalPlus. No revised seed-reporting, repeated-training-run or uncertainty-estimation procedure is documented.

E6.justification: Matched benchmark and original ablation scores are unchanged, but substantial new results appear in v3 Figure 4 and Tables 7–9 and 11. For example, Table 7 reports DS-1.3B ordering-error averages of 9.91% without HLP versus 6.68% with HLP; Table 11 reports self-infilling scores of 31.7 versus 32.9 at four loops. These are new comparisons, not version-to-version performance gains. Training-set R2 entries from v2 Table 7 are omitted, while test scores remain.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(5), including the horizon target and training losses, are unchanged. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs. The added diagnostic criteria and mechanism discussion concern empirical evaluation and interpretation.

C1.justification: The central claims remain: HLP teaches horizon awareness, improves FIM by up to 24% relatively without dataset-specific post-processing, benefits code reasoning, and adds negligible training overhead with no inference overhead. Rewritten contribution bullets emphasize additional supporting analyses without changing these claims' substance.

C2.justification: v3 expands the mechanism explanation into length-aware subgoals and interprets increased suffix attention and fewer ordering errors as evidence of proactive planning. It adds loss-weight saturation and self-infilling interpretations, plus explicit limitations concerning models above 7B parameters and non-code domains. The existing L2R-degradation discussion remains.

D1.justification: v3 documents the new sweep's 100K-step budget, logistic activation for the nonlinear probe, and self-infilling loop procedure. However, it omits v2's 3,000-step warm-up disclosure and replaces the precise the-stack-v2-train-smol identifier with the broader the-stack-v2 description. These omissions do not establish actual training changes.

R1.justification: v3 adds Zheng et al.'s Self-infilling Code Generation and connects HLP to that approach. It removes the Brown et al. (2020) and Kang et al. (2024) citations. Positioning against standard FIM, lookahead decoding and multi-token prediction otherwise remains stable.

P1.justification: The title changes to Planning-Aware Code Infilling via Horizon-Length Prediction. The abstract, introduction and explanatory passages are extensively rewritten; the discussion is reorganized, the multi-token comparison moves to the appendix, and the appendix sequence is substantially restructured.

P2.justification: The document changes from predominantly single-column to two-column layout, extensively relocating and resizing displays. v2 Figure 1 is removed; its Figure 2 becomes a vertically arranged first-page example. v3 adds an attention plot and four tables, and transposes the linear-probing table while dropping its training-results column.

improvement.justification: The added ordering-error analysis, nonlinear probe and loss-weight sweep strengthen support for the planning hypothesis beyond v2's existing probes and ablations, while explicit limitations clarify applicability. These useful gains are tempered by reduced training-detail disclosure and an overstatement in the self-infilling discussion: v3 Table 11 shows a tie at two loops despite claiming consistent outperformance.
